text: A Deployment's Pods are interchangeable on purpose. Scale from three replicas to five, and the new Pods get randomly suffixed names with no guaranteed identity; scale back down, and any one of the five might be removed. That's right for a stateless API server. It's wrong for a clustered database, where node zero and node one play genuinely different roles and each needs its own data directory, not a shared or randomly swapped one.

A StatefulSet gives you two guarantees a Deployment doesn't. First, stable, predictable Pod names: a StatefulSet named postgres with three replicas creates Pods literally named postgres-0, postgres-1, postgres-2, keeping that exact name across restarts. Paired with a headless Service, each one also gets its own resolvable DNS name. Second, a dedicated PersistentVolumeClaim per replica, created from a template rather than shared.

That second guarantee comes from volumeClaimTemplates, and it's the field that solves the problem from two lessons ago, where every replica tried to mount the same ReadWriteOnce PVC. Instead of one shared volumes block, Kubernetes stamps out one PVC per replica, named by convention pgdata-postgres-0, pgdata-postgres-1, and so on — postgres-1 never touches postgres-0's disk.

Delete postgres-1 — a node failure, a manual restart, doesn't matter — and the StatefulSet recreates a Pod with that exact same name, which reattaches to that exact same pgdata-postgres-1 claim and the data already sitting on it. That's the guarantee a clustered, stateful workload actually needs, and precisely what a Deployment's interchangeable Pods cannot provide.

By default, a StatefulSet also starts and scales its Pods in order, one at a time — postgres-0 must be Running and Ready before postgres-1 is even created — and scales down in reverse, removing the highest-numbered replica first. Many database operators assume exactly this ordering, since replica zero often bootstraps a cluster the later replicas join.

serviceName is mandatory too, pointing at a headless Service with clusterIP: None, which is what makes each Pod individually addressable instead of load-balanced. With identity and per-replica storage both solved, the real question left is operational: is running the actual database engine inside that StatefulSet the right call, which is exactly what closes out this chapter.
